text: Something is coveted when lots of people want it badly — often more than they can actually get. Pineapples were once so coveted in England that people who couldn't afford to buy one would rent one, just to show it off at dinner.

To anticipate something is to expect it before it happens and get ready for it. Food companies try to anticipate the next big craze so they can buy up ingredients before rival companies even notice the trend starting.
Novelty is the quality of being new and different, and the excitement that comes with it. Young buyers love novelty, which is why a brand-new drink nobody has tried yet can take off online so fast.
The watery liquid left over when milk is turned into cheese. Dried into a powder, it is packed with protein — that is what goes into gym shakes and protein bars.

Those who eat, drink, or use something up. Funny enough, the first consumers in this article are pigs — they used to eat most of the whey. In business talk, consumers usually means the people who buy things.
Something extra that gets made while you are making something else. Whey is a byproduct of cheesemaking: the cheese is the goal, and the whey just comes along with it.
Barely; almost not at all. Farmers can scarcely afford whey now — meaning they almost cannot afford it — because its price has jumped so high.
Here this is not about bossing someone around. In economics, demand means how much of something people want to buy. When demand jumps and there isn't enough to go around, prices climb.
Here this is not about focusing your mind. A concentrate is a thickened or powdered form of something, with the water taken out — whey concentrate is whey dried down into a strong protein powder.
Here firm is not about being hard or solid — a firm is simply a company. Vesper, the research firm in the article, is a company that studies food prices.
Farms or factories that handle milk and turn it into products like cheese, butter, and yogurt. Dairies make whey as a side effect of making cheese.
Gym slang for building bigger muscles by eating lots of protein and lifting weights. TikTok fitness stars recommend cottage cheese for bulking up, which helped cause a shortage of it.
Here it does not mean drawing pictures. When examples illustrate a problem, they show it clearly — the whey and cottage-cheese shortages both show the same problem in action.
In business, to scale production (or scale it up) means to grow it to a much bigger size. Farms and factories cannot scale as fast as an online trend spreads — you can't triple a farm overnight.

To ride out something is to get through it and last until it ends, like a ship riding out a storm. Companies try to ride out food trends — make money from them while they last, before shoppers move on.

A fad is something wildly popular for a short time that then fades away, like a dance move or a toy everyone suddenly must have. This article is about food fads — from fondue in the 1970s to matcha today.
England in the 1700s and early 1800s, when four kings named George ruled one after another. Back then a pineapple was a rare luxury that showed everyone how rich you were.
Selling things by offering them around, often small goods. Shops in Georgian England peddled display pineapples — renting out fruit for people to show off, not eat.

A dish from Switzerland: a pot of melted cheese that you dip bread into with long forks. It was a huge fad in America in the 1960s and 70s — then millions of fondue pots ended up forgotten in cupboards.
To sit unused and forgotten, slowly fading away. All those fondue pots now languish in cupboards — nobody melts cheese in them anymore.

When a video or idea goes viral, it spreads across the internet extremely fast, like a virus jumping from person to person. The Dubai chocolate-bar video went viral and was watched more than 100 million times.
People or companies that make fine chocolate — it comes from the French word for chocolate makers. After the Dubai bar went viral, top chocolatiers rushed to sell their own versions.
Putting heavy pressure on something, stretching it close to its limit. All those new pistachio chocolate bars were straining pistachio production — the farms could barely keep up.
Likely to do something or have something happen to it. Food and drinks are prone to going viral — they go viral more easily than most other products do.
A bright-green powder made from finely ground Japanese tea leaves, whisked into drinks like lattes. Its striking grass-green color helped make it an internet star.
A purple sweet potato from the Philippines with a sweet, nutty taste. Its bright violet color makes drinks and desserts look amazing in photos — a big part of why it became a fad.
Easy for ordinary people to get or afford. A trendy latte is accessible — almost anyone can spare a few dollars to try one, unlike a fancy gadget that costs hundreds.
To cost more than you can afford. Even a $19 strawberry won't break the bank — it is a lot for one strawberry, but most people could pay it once for the fun of it.
Tending to like or lean toward something. Young buyers are inclined towards novelty — given a choice, they will usually pick the new thing over the familiar one.
The special shade-grown tea leaves that get ground up into matcha powder. The bushes they grow on take years to mature, so farmers cannot quickly grow more when demand explodes.
Rising fast and powerfully, like a wave. Surging interest in matcha means the number of people wanting it shot up very quickly.
A British word for people who jump at any chance to make quick money, even if they don't really know the business. When matcha got hot, the market filled up with chancers hoping to profit.
People who stand between the maker and the buyer: they buy from farmers, then resell to shops or customers. Every middleman takes a cut of the money, which can push prices up.
To go between two sides and help them deal with each other. The new middlemen hoped to mediate between Japanese tea farmers and buyers in other countries — and charge for the service.
People who start their own businesses, taking on the risk themselves in hopes of making money. Japanese entrepreneurs rushed into the matcha trade when prices started rising.
To secure something firmly so nobody else can take it. By spotting a trend early, a company can lock in suppliers — sign deals for the ingredients before rival companies even try.
Here a chain is a company that runs many matching stores or restaurants under one name, like Starbucks or Shake Shack. Each store in the chain looks and works about the same.
Made something popular that few people knew about before — this is the British spelling of popularized. Starbucks popularised drinks with popping pearls before bubble tea was everywhere.
A coffee drink made with espresso and smooth steamed milk — a bit like a small, stronger latte. It started in Australia and New Zealand and is now standard in cafes across Europe.
Small groups of ordinary people that a company gathers in a room to ask what they think of a product. Starbucks used to rely on focus groups; now it tracks millions of customers online instead.
Extremely popular and fashionable right now. When spicy foods became all the rage in 2022, fast-food chains raced to add heat to their menus.
Literally, embracing someone is hugging them — but here it means accepting something eagerly and making it part of what you do. Not every fad is worth embracing; some are better left alone.
Something that makes you need the bathroom — it loosens your insides. Customers complained that Starbucks' olive-oil coffee had laxative effects, which helped get it pulled from menus.
In the middle of, or while something is going on. Prices rose amid the protein craze — meaning the rise happened during, and because of, the craze.
